---
title: "Quiz: normalising flows"
---

Short questions on the change of variables, coupling layers and the uses and limits of flows. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** Noise $z \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)$ is mapped to $x = 3z$. At $x = 0$, is the density of $x$ higher or lower than that of $z$ at $z = 0$, and by what factor?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The map stretches by 3.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Lower, by a factor 3: $p_X(0) = p_Z(0)/3 = 0.399/3 = 0.133$. The same probability is spread over three times the length.
:::

---

**Q2.** Why can a coupling layer be inverted even though its small network $s, t$ (a ReLU network, say) cannot?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is the input of $s$ and $t$, and is it known during the inverse?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$s$ and $t$ only see the kept half $x_1$, which passes through unchanged: $y_1 = x_1$. In the inverse, $y_1$ is known, so $s(y_1)$ and $t(y_1)$ are simply recomputed (a forward pass), and $x_2 = (y_2 - t)\,e^{-s}$. The network is never inverted.
:::

---

**Q3.** A coupling layer has $s = (0.5, -0.2, 0.1)$ for the three numbers it changes. What is its log-determinant, and does it expand or shrink volume?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\log|\det J| = \sum s$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$0.5 - 0.2 + 0.1 = 0.4$; $e^{0.4} = 1.49 > 1$: it expands volume by about half.
:::

---

**Q4.** What does a flow give that a VAE and a GAN do not?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Think of $\log p(x)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The exact log-likelihood $\log p(x)$ of any point (the VAE gives a lower bound, the GAN nothing), together with sampling in one pass and an exact inverse (an encoding $z = f(x)$ that loses nothing).
:::

---

**Q5.** A flow trained on images of healthy cells assigns a very high likelihood to a nearly empty, smooth image. Is that image a typical healthy cell?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What makes an image "easy" for a density model?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. Smooth, low-detail images get high likelihood because they have little to code, not because they look like the training data. Likelihood is not typicality: an anomaly score from a flow must be tested on known anomalies.
:::

---

**Q6.** Why does a flow trained on two separated clusters leave a thin trail of probability between them?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Can a smooth invertible map turn one connected blob into two pieces?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A continuous invertible map keeps connected sets connected. The Gaussian is one blob, so its image stays connected: the flow can make the bridge between the clusters very thin, but not remove it.
:::

---

**Q7.** *(math)* Two layers with Jacobians $J_1$ and $J_2$ are applied one after the other. What is the log-determinant of the whole map?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Chain rule, then $\det(AB) = \det A\det B$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The Jacobian is $J_2J_1$ (each evaluated at its own input), so $\log|\det| = \log|\det J_1| + \log|\det J_2|$: log-determinants add over layers.
:::
